mcqs.question: What is the core modeling idea behind state-machine DP, as used in the stock problems?
options: Each day is placed in one of a small number of explicit states, and a recurrence is written for how the best value in each state transitions from the previous day
Every day's decision is made independently of all other days
The problem must be reformulated as a graph shortest-path problem
State-machine DP only applies when there are exactly two possible actions per day
mcqs.explanation: The technique is to enumerate the qualitatively different modes a process can be in (here: holding a share or not), then write one recurrence per state describing how it's reached from the previous day's states via legal transitions — that generalizes well beyond just two actions.

mcqs.question: Why does the unlimited-transactions stock problem reduce to a simple greedy sum of positive daily deltas, while the one-transaction version needs to track running state?
options: Because unlimited transactions always produce a smaller profit than one transaction
Because with no cap and no cost per transaction, no earlier buy/sell decision ever forecloses a later opportunity, so each day's local up/down comparison is always safe
Because the unlimited version is actually a harder problem requiring more state, not less
Because the one-transaction version doesn't have well-defined states
mcqs.explanation: With unlimited transactions and no constraints tying them together, capturing every profitable up-move independently is always optimal — no earlier choice can hurt a later one. The one-transaction version needs to track the best cost basis so far because it has a genuine constraint (only one buy, one sell) that ties decisions together across days.

mcqs.question: Adding a mandatory cooldown after selling requires introducing a third state beyond hold and sold. Why can't the existing two-state model handle it with just a modified transition?
options: Because cooldown always requires switching to a 2D array over days and prices
Because the recurrence needs to distinguish 'not holding, free to buy today' from 'not holding, but still in cooldown' — a distinction the two original states can't express
Because cooldown makes the problem unsolvable with DP
Because cooldown only affects the very first transaction, not later ones
mcqs.explanation: The original two states only capture 'holding' vs. 'not holding' — they can't distinguish two different flavors of 'not holding' that now behave differently (one can buy immediately, one can't). A genuinely new condition the answer depends on requires a genuinely new state, not a patched transition.

mcqs.question: Why does the at-most-k-transactions variant add a transaction-count dimension to the state instead of just tracking a running total separately?
options: Because the answer at a given day and holding-status genuinely differs depending on how many transactions have been used, so that count must be part of the state the DP indexes over, not an external counter
Because k transactions always requires a completely different algorithm unrelated to the base problem
Tracking it separately would work identically and is just a stylistic choice
Because the price array must be sorted first when a transaction limit is introduced
mcqs.explanation: The best achievable profit at a given day and holding state depends on how many transactions remain, so two situations with the same day and holding status but different transaction counts can have genuinely different correct answers — that's exactly what forces the count into the state itself rather than being tracked as a side variable.

mcqs.question: You apply the 'sum every profitable up-move' greedy shortcut to a stock problem that has a transaction fee. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing — the greedy shortcut is fee-agnostic and still gives the optimal answer
The shortcut overcounts profit, because it assumes every profitable move is free to capture, but a fee can make slicing a big gain into many small transactions net-negative
The shortcut undercounts profit by exactly the total fee amount, which can simply be subtracted afterward
The shortcut only breaks when prices are strictly decreasing
mcqs.explanation: The greedy shortcut relies on transactions being free and unconstrained, which is exactly what a fee breaks — capturing every tiny up-move can rack up more fees than the gains are worth, so the optimal strategy under a fee sometimes holds through small dips it would have sold at fee-free. Subtracting a flat total fee after the fact doesn't fix this, since the fee applies per transaction, not once overall.
